title: Month 29
subtitle: The thirty-month visit is next month. It is short, and it is the last one before three.

baby.development: Your child says three words together, can jump, and is starting to run around obstacles. They can name a friend and are beginning to take turns with help.

you.body: If you are pregnant again, the birth plan needs a plan for the two-year-old. Who takes them, and where.
you.mind: Twenty-nine months is when the child starts to have a friend rather than a playmate. It is a small and real thing.

coreActions.title: Book the thirty-month visit
coreActions.why: This is a short developmental check, and it is the last visit before the three-year check.
coreActions.detail: The thirty-month visit usually has no vaccines. The doctor will check language, movement, and teeth, and will ask about sleep, eating, and toilet learning. Write the questions down before you go.

coreActions.title: Practise taking turns with a timer
coreActions.why: Taking turns is a skill that is taught, and a timer makes the waiting concrete in a way that a sentence does not.
coreActions.detail: Use a two-minute timer. One child has the toy until it rings, then the other. Stay close and narrate. A two-year-old cannot wait long, so keep the turns short. This is the foundation for sharing at three.

coreActions.title: Teach their own name
coreActions.why: Knowing their own name is a safety skill as well as a language one, and it is what a preschool teacher will ask for.
coreActions.detail: Say the name in songs and in play. Ask who is this in the mirror. Point at their photo. A child who can say their first name by three is on track. A surname comes later.

alsoKnow.title: A dental visit every six months
alsoKnow.body: From two, a check every six months is the usual schedule. A first visit may have happened already; if not, it is worth booking now.

alsoKnow.title: Eleven to fourteen hours, including the nap
alsoKnow.body: A two-and-a-half-year-old usually sleeps eleven to fourteen hours a day, including one nap. Night waking is still common and is not a sign of a problem.

redFlags.text: Choking — cannot breathe, cough, or make a sound
A fever over 100.4°F with unusual sleepiness or a rash
A fall from furniture, or a head injury with vomiting or unusual sleepiness
